segments.text: Chemical analysis usually requires isolating one component from a complex mixture before it can be identified or measured. Separation methods exploit small physical or chemical differences between components — solubility, polarity, charge, or size — to achieve this.
separates a compound based on its differing solubility in two immiscible liquids (e.g., water and an organic solvent). The

describes the equilibrium ratio of a solute’s concentration between the two phases at a given temperature; a large partition coefficient favours extraction into the chosen solvent. Repeated extractions with fresh solvent achieve better recovery than a single extraction with the same total solvent volume, because equilibrium is re-established each time.

— separation occurs because each component partitions differently between the two phases (a direct application of the partitioning idea above). Common forms include paper chromatography (stationary phase: paper/water), thin-layer chromatography (TLC; stationary phase: a thin adsorbent layer), and column chromatography (stationary phase packed into a column, allowing larger-scale or automated separation, including gas and liquid chromatography variants used for precise quantitative analysis).

separates charged species (commonly biomolecules like proteins or DNA fragments) by their differing migration rates through a medium under an applied electric field — migration rate depends on the charge-to-size ratio, so smaller or more highly charged species move faster.

blocks.text: 4. Choice of phases and separation efficiency

segments.text: Selecting appropriate stationary and mobile phases is the central practical decision in any chromatographic separation: phases are chosen so that the components of interest have sufficiently different partition behaviour to separate cleanly within a reasonable time.

(in column techniques) — greater differences between components’ retention values indicate better resolution.

Interpreting a chromatogram or electropherogram means relating the position, retention value, or migration distance of each spot or peak to a known standard (for identification) and its size or intensity to the amount present (for quantification) — connecting this chapter’s techniques directly to the calibration principles of Chemometrics (Chapter 6).

items.text: Solvent extraction relies on differing solubility (partition coefficient) between two immiscible phases; repeated smaller extractions outperform one large extraction.

Chromatography generalises the same partitioning principle to a moving mobile phase over a stationary phase, with paper, TLC, and column/gas/liquid variants suited to different scales and precision needs.
Electrophoresis separates charged species by migration rate under an electric field, dependent on charge-to-size ratio.
Retention factor/time quantifies separation efficiency, and comparing sample results to known standards enables both identification and quantification.
